answer_text: Under the GDPR, a controller must act within one month of receipt of the request, and this period may be extended by two further months where necessary due to complexity or number of requests.
The prohibitions apply from 2 February 2025, and the Regulation applies in general from 2 August 2026.
The provider must publish at least once every six months, and the average is calculated over the past six months.
The trader must deliver the goods not more than 30 days after the day on which the contract is entered into.

Pre-ticked boxes are not valid consent, and requiring withdrawal only by signed letter is not acceptable under the GDPR.

- Pre-ticked boxes do not constitute consent because consent requires a clear affirmative act; silence or pre-ticked boxes should not constitute consent (Recital 32, evidence 1 and 2).
- Withdrawal of consent must be as easy as giving it; since the sign-up uses a simple tick, requiring a signed letter makes withdrawal harder and thus violates Article 7(3) (Article 7(3), evidence 3 and 4).

The university lab's use is not caught by the prohibition, but the retailer's use is caught.

- The AI Act excludes AI systems developed and put into service solely for scientific research (Evidence [3]).
- The retailer's use of the same system to monitor staff mood falls under the prohibition in Article 5(f) because it infers emotions in the workplace (Evidence [1]).
- Emotion recognition is defined as identifying or inferring emotions such as happiness or sadness from biometric data (Evidence [5]).
- No exception for medical or safety reasons applies to the retailer's scenario (Evidence [1]).

The platform must inform the user of the removal decision. The user can challenge it through the internal complaint system for at least six months, starting from the day the user is informed, and at no cost (free of charge).

- Article 20(1) requires the platform to provide access to an internal complaint-handling system, electronically and free of charge, against decisions to remove or disable access.
- Article 20(2) states the six-month period starts on the day the user is informed about the decision in accordance with Article 16(5) or Article 17.
- Article 20(1)(a) explicitly covers decisions whether to remove or disable access to information.

No, the consumer cannot use the short-term right to reject because the 30‑day time limit has passed (section 22(3)). The next remedy is the right to repair or replacement under section 19(3)(b) and section 23. The consumer does not have to prove the fault existed at delivery; under section 19(14), goods that do not conform within six months are presumed not to have conformed on the day of delivery. Section 22(3) sets the time limit at 30 days from delivery, and the laptop was delivered ten weeks ago, so the right is lost. Section 19(3) gives the right to repair or replacement for goods not of satisfactory quality. Section 19(14) creates a presumption of non-conformity at delivery for failures appearing within six months.

DSA - counts: average monthly active recipients of the service (online platforms or online search engines) in the Union equal to or higher than 45 million.  
DMA - counts: monthly active end users (for a core platform service) in the Union at least 45 million, and additionally requires at least 10,000 yearly active business users established in the Union.

The DSA counts recipients of the service (users of the platform/search engine), while the DMA counts end users of a core platform service and adds a separate threshold for business users (at least 10,000 yearly active).

Digital Markets Act: 10%
Digital Services Act: 6%
Artificial Intelligence Act: 7%
The values are not directly comparable as they apply to different violations under different regulations.

AI Act (general case) - 15 days
GDPR (where feasible) - 72 hours
The GDPR deadline of 72 hours is shorter than the AI Act's 15 days.
